subtitle: Part 1: Expectancy
title: 6 Steps to Profitable Swing Trading
body_html:
While there are undoubtedly many ways to swing trade, what follows is my 6-step method to understanding my system and the market’s impact on that system; knowing when the odds are in my favor; finding the fastest horses; finding low-risk ways to get on the horse; risk management strategies; and position management strategies.

Step 1: What can I reasonably expect?

Many traders become overly fixated on chart patterns and indicators, believing that discovering the perfect pattern or the optimal settings for their indicators will lead to substantial profits. Consequently, they constantly jump from one setup to another, from one system to another, and from one indicator to another in search of that elusive Holy Grail that promises consistent gains week after week, year after year. They may switch from the 10EMA to the 13EMA or adjust the MACD settings from 12, 9, 26 to 11, 15, 22 based on the recommendations of so-called experts. In the end, they end up using numerous indicators in layers, hoping that this will give them the confidence to outsmart other market participants and make profitable trades.

It's important to understand that these tools are designed to help traders identify situations that offer high rewards with low risk. However, most traders fail to recognize that certain indicators and setups are only effective in specific market environments. For example, a breakout or pullback setup may be highly profitable during a bullish market, but when the market becomes choppy or bearish, these same setups may fail to deliver results.

It's critical to realize that finding high-reward, low-risk situations is just one part of the equation. It's equally important to know when a particular setup is most effective and when it's not. This understanding is guided by the concept of expectancy and how expectancy variables change when market conditions change. So, it's vital to keep this in mind while analyzing indicators and setups to ensure that you're making informed trading decisions.

What is expectancy?

While most people focus on balancing their profit/loss ratios or on the accuracy of their trading approach, they are unaware that a bigger picture exists: Your trading performance depends largely on your expectancy, which is:

(Avg Win * Win Rate) - (Avg Loss * Loss Rate)

For example, if your average trade wins $200, the average loss is $100, and your batting average is 50%, then your expectancy is ($200 * .5) - ($100 * .5) = $50

This means that for every trade you place with these ratios, you can expect to earn $50 on average per trade over a series of trades.

Add in frequency and you get the actual performance over X number of trades. So with a positive expectancy of $50, if you took 100 trades in a month, your theoretical performance is $5,000. If you only took 5 trades in a month, then $250.

So as you can see, performance is a three-legged stool, and all of the variables are important. You can’t accurately assess a system’s performance by just talking about profit/loss ratios or batting averages. A system with $100 winners and $300 losers sounds awful, but this system can still produce positive results based on the math. Don’t believe me?

($100 * .80) - ($300 * .20) = $20

It's possible for a trading system to produce profits even if it has losses that are three times larger than its wins. For example, if the system is executed over 100 trades, it can still generate $2,000 in profits, despite having an unfavorable R ratio. Traders who are too focused on R values may overlook other sources of an edge.

Frequency and accuracy are also crucial factors that contribute to an edge. Even if a trader has only a 2 or 3% edge, they can still make significant profits if the frequency of trades is high enough. This is similar to how casinos operate. Their edge may be small, but over thousands of hands and millions of dollars wagered, they know that they will come out ahead at the end of the night, after all the big winners and losers have been accounted for.

Therefore, traders should not solely rely on R ratios, but instead, consider all aspects that contribute to their edge. By doing so, they can increase their chances of making profitable trades and achieving long-term success in the market by understanding the expectancy related to their system and setups.

How do you know your expectancy?

Tracking your trades.

Link: Trade Log

The link will take you to a trading log that has pre-built formulas. As you enter your trade information, the top portion will auto-update to show BA, expectancy, avg win,, avg loss, etc. Fuck with the parameters at your own risk.

Once you’ve logged 20-30 trades, you should start getting a good idea, setup by setup, how your systems and setups are performing. This objective data is important to capture since you can’t reasonably move forward without knowing these values.

In Part 2 of the series, we will explore how different market environments affect different parts of the expectancy formula and why it is critical to your success that you understand this.

Stay Tuned!!
